title: US targets overseas computing used by Chinese firms

needs.need: Which operators the computing-access licensing reaches: data centers anywhere, not only in the five chip-rule countries.
needs.inStory: It also set licensing requirements for overseas data centers supplying substantial computing capacity to firms headquartered in China or other restricted countries.
needs.accepts: A named source distinguishing the five-country chip-export licensing from the computing-access licensing, which applies to large data-center operators anywhere in the world serving China-headquartered or other restricted customers.

example.value: The chip rule names Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, while the computing-access rule requires a license for large data-center operators anywhere in the world to serve companies headquartered in China.

needs.need: What changes for Chinese firms using advanced American chips located abroad.
needs.inStory: Until the rule change, overseas facilities could lawfully sell computing capacity to Chinese tech firms.
needs.accepts: A named source contrasting the previously lawful supply of overseas computing to Chinese firms with the new license requirement for covered services. Saying export controls have tightened does not meet it.

example.value: Before November 16 it had not been illegal for overseas data centers to provide computing power to Chinese tech firms.

needs.need: What obligations the US now imposes to stop overseas data centers from serving restricted users.
needs.inStory: Operators serving companies in countries such as China, Russia, Iran and Cuba must identify their end users.
needs.accepts: A named source identifying the license requirement for covered computing services and the end-user identification requirement. It must not present their effectiveness at stopping diversion as established.

example.value: Overseas data centers providing services to companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba must identify their end users.

needs.inStory: Data centers already serving companies in restricted countries have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to apply for a license.
needs.accepts: A named source stating that data centers already serving restricted-country firms have 90 days from the rule's effective date to obtain a license.

example.value: Data centers already serving such companies will have 90 days from the rule's effective date to get a license.

needs.need: What remote access to AI computing means when the chips stay outside China.
needs.inStory: the policy tests whether export controls can reach AI access when the hardware stays outside the restricted country
needs.accepts: A named source explaining that a customer can use computing on chips housed in a foreign data center to train or run AI models without importing the chips.

example.value: The rules seek to close loopholes that allow Chinese companies to rent computing capacity powered by American technology from facilities in third countries.

needs.need: What prompted the rules now: the suspected diversion case and the countries the US judges risky.
needs.accepts: A named source tying the rules to the scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed International, suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China, or to the US designation of the five countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. Megaspeed's conduct must be described as suspected, not proven.

example.value: The restrictions come amid scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US export controls.

needs.need: How the rules follow the 2022 controls and the 2025 reversal of the broader AI Diffusion Rule.
needs.accepts: A named source connecting the 2022 advanced-chip controls with the Trump administration's 2025 reversal of the AI Diffusion Rule, which would have required licenses for advanced-chip sales to much of Southeast Asia.

example.value: In 2025, the Trump administration reversed the AI Diffusion Rule, which would have required licenses for advanced chip sales to much of Southeast Asia.

notes: Story correction: the story says existing providers have 90 days to apply for a license; CNA and Fortune say 90 days to obtain one. A card giving 'obtain' is right, not a contradiction to mark down. Reports differ on whether the rule took effect on November 16 or on Federal Register publication; the date is not required.
